Manchester United completed the signing of Manuel Ugarte for €50m (£42m) plus €10m in bonuses from Paris Saint-Germain on Friday evening, with the Uruguayan promising to “fight for trophies” and help return the club to elite level. The 23-year-old signed a five-year contract with the option of a further 12 months. He is Erik ten Hag’s fifth major acquisition of the window and gives the manager a second senior No 6, alongside Casemiro.

Ugarte said: “It is an incredible feeling to join a club of this magnitude – one that is admired all around the world. The project that the football leadership discussed with me is extremely exciting. Manchester United is an ambitious club and I am an ambitious player. “I know how incredible United fans are and I cannot wait to experience Old Trafford. I’m someone who is so determined to succeed. I will sacrifice and give everything for my teammates. Together we will fight to win trophies and reach the level where this club needs to be.”

Dan Ashworth, United’s sporting director, said: “Signing Manuel was another of our primary targets for this summer. He brings a tenacity and intelligence that will be central to the structure Erik is building. His energy and defensive discipline are attributes we specifically sought to add to the squad.”

Later, as the ink on the contract dried and the camera lights dimmed, Erik ten Hag allowed himself a brief, satisfied smile. In his mind’s eye, he could already see the pieces slotting together on the tactical board. Last season, the burden on Casemiro had been immense. The Brazilian was a warrior, but by the final stretch of the season, the strain of single-handedly shielding the defence was apparent. Now, he had another warrior. A younger one, brimming with relentless stamina.

Ugarte’s first day at the Carrington training complex was quiet but intense. While some new arrivals might have been overawed, he moved with a quiet purpose. He sought out Casemiro first, not with the deference of a subordinate, but with the respect of a future partner.

“It is an honor to share the pitch with you,” Manuel said in a mix of Spanish and halting English.

Casemiro looked him up and down, a flicker of appraisal in his eyes. He saw the hunger. “The honor will be to win with you,” he replied, his tone serious. “This shirt is heavy. Be ready for the responsibility.”

The first training sessions were a revelation. Ugarte was a blur, an engine of perpetual motion. He wasn’t just a tackler; he was an interceptor, reading the game two steps ahead, appearing in passing lanes as if by magic. He treated every drill like the final minute of a cup final, his commitment causing even the most established veterans to raise their own intensity.

His debut came three weeks later, a chilly evening at Old Trafford against a notoriously difficult opponent. The game was locked in a tense midfield struggle. For seventy minutes, Ugarte was a whirlwind of controlled aggression, breaking up play and feeding crisp, simple passes to the more creative players ahead of him. The crowd, initially just appreciative, began to roar with every crunching but fair challenge.

Then came the moment. A swift counter-attack saw the opposition’s star striker glide past the last defender. The stadium held its breath. As the striker drew back his leg to shoot, a red blur slid across the damp grass. Ugarte, having covered an impossible amount of ground, hooked the ball cleanly away with the tip of his boot. It was a goal-saving, match-defining intervention. Old Trafford erupted in a wave of sound that was part relief, part adoration. He rose to his knees, pounded the crest on his chest, and roared back at the stands. He had made a promise to sacrifice, and here was the proof.

They won the match 1-0. In the dressing room afterward, as the celebrations wound down, Casemiro walked over and simply clapped him on the shoulder, a wide grin spreading across his face. It was a small gesture, but it meant everything. The project was real. The fight had begun.
